stimulus.text:
In August 1801, thousands of people gathered at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, for a six-day camp meeting led by the Presbyterian minister Barton W. Stone. Preachers from Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist churches preached at the same time from different platforms, and people wept, shouted, and fell to the ground as they were called to convert. Estimates put the crowd at 10,000 to 20,000 people, in a state whose whole population was about 220,000.

At the same time, some educated Americans followed deism, the belief that God created the world and then left it to run by natural laws, with no miracles and no revealed scripture.
stimulus.source_note: Cane Ridge account drawn from the Disciples Historical Society, Cane Ridge Revival, and the Revival of 1800; deism defined in standard terms.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from accounts of the Cane Ridge Revival, August 1801.

primary_sources: Barton W. Stone, account of the Cane Ridge meeting, August 1801

stem: The Cane Ridge meeting best illustrates which development in American religion around 1800?

options.text: The Second Great Awakening brought revival religion to ordinary frontier people.
The established churches of the colonies regained their old power over American life.
options.misconception: Cane Ridge mixed denominations outdoors, outside any established church’s control.

options.text: Most Americans in 1801 had stopped believing in God.
options.misconception: Thousands came to Cane Ridge to convert, which shows belief was strong, not fading.

options.text: The federal government began paying preachers to hold camp meetings.
options.misconception: Background: the government paid no preachers; the meeting was organized by churches, not by Congress.

rationales.A: Thousands of ordinary people gathered outdoors for days, hearing preachers of three churches call them to convert.
rationales.B: The meeting mixed Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist preachers, which no established church controlled.
rationales.C: A crowd of 10,000 to 20,000 seeking conversion shows strong belief, not unbelief.
rationales.D: The meeting was organized by a minister and churches, not paid for by the government.
rationales.general:
1. The meeting drew 10,000 to 20,000 people to an outdoor camp in Kentucky.
2. Preachers of three churches preached at once, and people wept and fell as they converted.
3. Background: this was the Second Great Awakening, whose revivals reached ordinary frontier people outside settled churches.
4. So Cane Ridge shows democratic, emotional revival religion reaching the frontier.
Remember: a revival’s size and setting can show who religion now reached.
